Designing a Payment Wallet Like PhonePe / Venmo / Cash App

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites:Saga Pattern, Event Sourcing, and Idempotency

TL;DR

A digital wallet is an accounting system disguised as a consumer app. Every transfer is a pair of debits and credits on a double-entry ledger. Money never moves without both sides of the entry being written atomically.💡 Double-entry ledger = every movement of money is written twice, once as leaving one account and once as arriving in another, and the two halves must cancel out. If they don’t, the write is refused - which is what makes “we lost a rupee” structurally impossible here.

In 3 sentences: Users load money from banks (async, webhook-confirmed), send to each other (instant, single DB transaction), and withdraw (async again). The core is a double-entry ledger in Postgres - every balance change creates both a debit and a credit line that sum to zero. Redis caches balances for fast reads; Kafka fans out events to notifications and analytics.

Understanding the Problem

👛 What is a payment wallet? A closed-loop or semi-closed-loop digital wallet lets users load money into a balance, send it peer-to-peer, pay merchants, and withdraw back to a bank. Examples: Paytm Wallet, PhonePe Wallet, Venmo, Cash App, Google Pay’s balance. Under the hood it’s an accounting system disguised as a consumer app - every “transfer” is a pair of debits and credits on a ledger, and every ₹1 or $1 moving in the app must correspond to real money sitting in a partner bank account.

Naive First Cut

30-second whiteboard sketch:

Store a balance column on the user row, UPDATE users SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE user_id = A and ... + 100 WHERE user_id = B. This breaks in every way that matters for money:

  • Race conditions on concurrent transfers corrupt balances.
  • No audit trail - who transferred what, when, why?
  • No way to reconcile against the real bank account.
  • A crash between the two updates creates or destroys money.
  • No idempotency → double-debits on retries.
  • No way to handle async outcomes (bank says “pending” for 3 seconds).

The rest of this doc evolves this into a system that a regulator, an auditor, and 360 million daily transactions can trust.

Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • Modern Treasury “Accounting for Developers” - the reference for how to model a Venmo-style wallet with double-entry: chart of accounts, debit-normal vs credit-normal accounts, balance = aggregate of entries. (source)
  • Uber “Gulfstream” - active-active payments with exactly-once via idempotency + strong consistency, double-entry bookkeeping, async stream processing of immutable orders. (source)
  • Airbnb “Orpheus” - idempotency framework with three-phase Pre-RPC / RPC / Post-RPC contract, retryable vs non-retryable error classification, and reads-from-primary-only to avoid replica-lag double-charges. (source)
  • PhonePe on Aerospike - 360M transactions/day served with sub-ms balance reads via a partitioned KV store; separated hot OLTP paths from governance/audit stores. (source)
  • TigerBeetle - purpose-built financial DB that enforces double-entry and debit/credit invariants at the storage layer itself; shows how far you can push correctness guarantees. (source)

Functional Requirements

Core Requirements

  1. Users can load money into the wallet from a bank, card, or UPI.
  2. Users can send money peer-to-peer to another wallet user.
  3. Users can withdraw to a bank account; users and internal systems can view balance and transaction history.

Below the line (out of scope)

  • Merchant payments with checkout flows (adjacent system)
  • Split bills, group payments, social feed
  • Rewards, cashback, subscriptions
  • KYC, sanctions screening, fraud scoring (assumed; not the design focus)
  • Cards issued against the wallet balance
  • Multi-currency, FX, international remittance
  • Interest / investment features

Non-Functional Requirements

Core Requirements

  • Correctness over everything. Money cannot be created, lost, or duplicated. Every rupee in a user’s balance must correspond to a rupee in our partner bank.
  • Strong consistency on the balance and ledger. Eventual is fine for history feed and analytics.
  • Low latency - P95 transfer under 500ms, balance check under 100ms.💡 P95 = the number that 95% of requests come in under, so “P95 under 500ms” means only the slowest 1 in 20 transfers is slower than half a second. P99 later in this design is the same idea for the slowest 1 in 100. Learn more →
  • High availability - 99.99% on the transfer path. Users block on this.
  • Auditability - every balance change is traceable to the ledger entries that produced it. Required for regulators and internal finance.
  • Idempotency - any operation is safe to retry without side effects.💡 Idempotency = running the same operation multiple times produces the same result. Essential for payment retries - charging a card twice would be catastrophic. Learn more →

Below the line

  • Globally multi-region active-active (single-region-primary with regional read replicas is fine to start)
  • Sub-100ms tail latencies (bounded by downstream banks and card rails anyway)

Scale Estimation (Back-of-Envelope)

  • Users: 50M DAU, 10M transactions/day
  • Write QPS: 500 txns/sec peak (double-entry = 1000 ledger writes/sec)💡 QPS = queries per second, the number of requests hitting a tier each second. Note the shape: writes are modest at 500/sec while balance reads are ten times that, and that asymmetry is the whole reason reads get their own cache later. Learn more →
  • Read QPS: 5K balance checks/sec, 2K transaction history queries/sec
  • Storage: ~1TB ledger data/year (immutable append-only entries)
  • Bandwidth: Zero tolerance for balance inconsistency - strong consistency on the write path

Core Entities

  • User - wallet holder, identified by phone/email, with know-your-customer (KYC) state.💡 KYC is the identity check a regulated financial product must run before letting someone move money. In this design it is just a state on the user that gates transfers.
  • Account - a logical bucket of money. Each user has one wallet account; the platform owns system accounts (cash-in-bank, fees-collected, etc.).
  • Journal Entry - a group of ledger lines representing a single logical transaction. All lines sum to zero.
  • Ledger Line - one debit or credit on one account, part of a journal entry. Append-only.
  • Transaction - the user-visible operation (load, send, withdraw). Owns a state machine and refers to its underlying journal entry.
  • Payment Instrument - a tokenized reference to a bank account, card, or UPI VPA the user has linked.

API / System Interface

POST /v1/wallets/:userId/load              → Transaction
     Body: { amount, paymentInstrumentId }
     Header: Idempotency-Key: <uuid>

POST /v1/transfers                         → Transaction
     Body: { toUserId, amount, note }
     Header: Idempotency-Key: <uuid>

POST /v1/wallets/:userId/withdraw          → Transaction
     Body: { amount, paymentInstrumentId }
     Header: Idempotency-Key: <uuid>

GET  /v1/wallets/:userId/balance           → { available, pending }
GET  /v1/wallets/:userId/transactions      → Transaction[]
GET  /v1/transactions/:id                  → Transaction

Security:

  • userId always comes from the authenticated JSON Web Token (JWT), never from a path or body for writes.💡 A JWT is a signed blob the client presents on every request; because we signed it, we can trust the user id inside it. Taking the user id from the request body instead would let anyone drain anyone’s wallet. Learn more →
  • Server computes the authoritative amount and fees; client-side numbers are advisory.
  • Every money-moving API requires an idempotency key.
  • Rate limit per user and per instrument to stop card-testing and credential stuffing.

High-Level Design

1) User loads money into the wallet

User adds ₹500 from their bank to their wallet. The interesting twist: this is inherently async, not by choice but because the payment rails we talk to (UPI, cards with 3DS, bank ACH) are themselves async.

Why we can’t make it sync:

Rail What has to happen Typical latency
UPI collect We request → NPCI → user’s bank app → user taps approve → bank debits → we’re told 5-30 seconds, sometimes minutes
Card with 3DS Authorize → bank issues OTP challenge → user enters OTP → bank confirms → we capture 10-60 seconds
Direct bank debit / ACH Authorize → bank runs its batch → settles Hours to days
scroll →

None of these are “call a function and get an answer in 200ms.” The shortest path still involves a human tapping a button in another app. If we held an open HTTP connection the whole time, thread pools would exhaust and P99 would balloon to 30s.

So the system accepts the request, returns 202 Processing immediately, and finds out the outcome when the rail tells us: the rail POSTs a signed callback to our webhook, referencing the txn_id we gave it when we started the charge.💡 A webhook is an HTTP endpoint we publish so somebody else’s system can call us when their work finishes, instead of us asking “done yet?” in a loop. The rail calls us; we do not wait on it.

Build that and nothing more. Four components and one Postgres table, where a user’s money is a balance column on their row. The double-entry ledger, the idempotency contract, the balance cache and the reconciliation machinery are all answers to the non-functional list — correctness, auditability, 100K QPS reads — so each is earned in a deep dive.

New components we need:

  1. API Gateway - authenticates users, applies rate limits, routes to the right service.
  2. Wallet Service - orchestrates loads. Writes the transaction row before calling any rail, so a crash still leaves evidence that we attempted a charge.
  3. Payment Gateway Adapter - translates our internal “charge this bank” into whatever each rail expects.💡 A universal translator between us and dozens of different bank APIs.
  4. Webhook Handler - receives the rail’s signed callback and applies the outcome.
  5. Postgres - a transactions row per attempt, and a users row carrying balance.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. User taps “Add ₹500 from HDFC Bank”
  2. The Wallet Service inserts a transactions row as PENDING before any network call — this row is our durable record that a charge was attempted
  3. It calls the Gateway Adapter, passing our txn_id as the reference so the callback can find its way back
  4. The rail accepts and promises to follow up; we return 202 Processing and the app shows “pending”
  5. Seconds or minutes later the user approves in their bank app
  6. The rail POSTs a signed callback; the Webhook Handler verifies the hash-based message authentication code (HMAC), because that endpoint is public and only signed payloads can be trusted💡 An HMAC is a short fingerprint computed from the message plus a secret only we and the rail know. Without it, anyone who finds this public URL could post “payment succeeded” and mint wallet balance.
  7. In one database transaction it adds ₹500 to the user’s balance and flips the row to SUCCEEDED

Why persist before calling the bank? If we called first and crashed before writing anything, money could leave the user’s account with no record on our side that we ever asked for it — an unrecoverable position, because there is nothing to investigate from. Write first, call second is the one rule payment systems do not bend.

What we have deliberately left broken. Money arrives and lands in the right wallet. Four things are wrong, and this is a domain where each of them is the sort that ends up in front of a regulator:

  • balance is a number that cannot explain itself. Asked why a user holds ₹4,320 the only answer is “the column says so”. No history, no derivation, nothing to audit — and the requirements open with correctness above everything and auditability as a named target. That is Deep Dive 1.
  • A retry adds the money twice. Nothing marks the intent, so a client that resends after a timeout gets a second charge and a second credit. That is Deep Dive 5.
  • If the callback in step 6 never arrives, the transaction is stuck forever. The rail is the only thing that knows the truth and we only ever learn it by being told. A dropped webhook leaves a permanently PENDING row and a user whose money has left their bank and not appeared in their wallet. Deep Dive 4 is where we stop depending on being told.
  • Nothing checks that the money is really there. We credit the wallet on the strength of a callback. Whether our partner bank actually holds the rupees we claim our users own is never verified. That is also Deep Dive 4.

2) User sends money to another wallet user

Pure internal transfer - no bank rail involved. Fastest and most common operation.

No rail is involved, so nothing here is async. Both wallets are rows in the same database, which makes this the simplest operation in the system: check the sender can afford it, then move the number.

New components we need:

  1. Transfer Service - validates the sender’s balance, that the recipient exists, and the daily limits, then applies the transfer.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Sender taps “Send ₹100 to Priya”
  2. The Transfer Service checks the obvious things: does Priya exist, is the sender KYC-verified, is this not a self-transfer, is it inside the daily limit
  3. It reads the sender’s balance and confirms it is at least ₹100
  4. In one database transaction it subtracts ₹100 from the sender and adds ₹100 to Priya, and writes a transactions row
  5. It returns the sender’s new balance, comfortably inside the 500ms P95 target

Why one database transaction rather than a saga? Because both wallets live in the same Postgres instance, so atomicity is free. Either both updates commit or neither does, with no distributed coordination, no compensating rollback, and no window where the money exists in neither place. Reaching for a saga here would be inventing a distributed problem we do not have.💡 Saga = a sequence of local transactions each with a compensating undo, used when the steps span systems that cannot share one transaction.

What we have deliberately left broken. The transfer is atomic and the decision to allow it is not:

  • Steps 3 and 4 are separate. The balance is read, then written, with no lock between. A user with ₹100 who taps “send ₹80” and “send ₹50” in quick succession has both requests land on different pods, both read ₹100, both conclude there are sufficient funds, and both commit. She has now sent ₹130 she did not have, and the wallet has created ₹30 out of nothing — which the requirements name as the one thing that must never happen. That is Deep Dive 2.
  • A retried request sends the money twice. As in FR1, nothing identifies the intent, so a dropped response and a client retry is a second transfer. That is Deep Dive 5.

3) Balance and transaction history

Both of these are already sitting in the database. The balance is the column FR1 and FR2 have been updating, and the history is the transactions rows they have been writing.

New components we need:

  1. Read Service - serves the balance and the transaction list.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. User opens the app, which asks for their balance
  2. The Read Service selects balance from the user’s row — one primary-key read
  3. The user scrolls to history; the service reads the most recent transactions rows for that user, ordered by time
  4. Both come back well inside the 100ms balance-check target

Why is the balance a single column read rather than a computation? Because it gates spending. Every transfer in FR2 checks it before allowing money to move, so it has to be available in a single cheap read on the critical path. Deriving it would make the most frequent read in the system also the most expensive one.

What we have deliberately left broken. These reads are correct and they are about to become the busiest thing we do:

  • Every screen in the app checks the balance. The requirements put this at 100K+ QPS against a 100ms target, all landing on the same Postgres primary that FR1 and FR2 write to, and overwhelmingly returning a number that has not changed since the last time it was asked for. That is Deep Dive 3.
  • The history read gets slower for exactly the users we most want to keep. transactions grows forever and is never partitioned, so a customer with five years of activity pays for all of it every time they scroll. Deep Dive 3 is also where the read path stops sharing a store with the write path.
  • One balance cannot express money that is not yet spendable. A load that the bank still calls pending is added straight to balance in FR1 step 7, so the user can immediately spend money we have not actually received. That is Deep Dive 6.

Technology Choices

Each data tier has a different job. Picking one DB to “just store everything” is the mistake that kills most wallet prototypes. Here’s what each tier does and what actually fits.

Tier What it stores Access pattern Primary pick Alternatives
Ledger (source of truth) journal_entries, ledger_lines, accounts, transactions - append-only, ACID required Point writes (inserts only), point reads, SELECT FOR UPDATE on balance rows PostgreSQL with partitioning by month on ledger_lines MySQL / Aurora, CockroachDB for multi-region strong consistency, TigerBeetle for invariant-enforced financial storage
Balance cache balance:{userId} → current available + pending 100K+ point reads/sec, invalidate on ledger write Redis (cluster mode) Memcached, Valkey, Aerospike at PhonePe scale
Idempotency keys idem:{merchantOrUser}:{endpoint}:{hash} → response JSON SET NX PX, retrieval on retry, short TTL Redis (same cluster as balance cache, separate keyspace) DynamoDB with TTL if you want it durable by default
Transaction history feed denormalized per-user transaction list for the history screen Range scans by (user_id, created_at DESC) at hundreds of QPS Cassandra or ClickHouse DynamoDB with user_id PK and created_at sort key
Event bus (outbox fan-out) transaction.succeeded, rail.confirmed events Ordered per-key, replayable, at least once Kafka Kinesis, Google Pub/Sub, Pulsar
CDC Postgres WAL → Kafka Continuous Debezium Native logical replication + custom publisher
Raw events lake Every event forever, for audit and ML Append-only, columnar for ad-hoc queries S3 + Parquet via Kafka S3 sink GCS, Azure Blob, MinIO
Ad-hoc analytics SQL over raw events Infrequent, high-scan Athena / Trino / BigQuery Snowflake, DuckDB
Settlement / reconciliation store daily settlement files, bank statements, reconciliation breaks Append, compare, query by day Postgres (separate schema from OLTP) Same-cluster Postgres is fine; doesn’t need scale
KYC / user profile Name, phone, docs, tier, limits Point lookup by user_id Postgres DynamoDB
scroll →

Why Postgres for the ledger (not DynamoDB or Cassandra):

  • The ledger is where correctness lives. We need multi-row ACID transactions (insert journal entry + 2+ ledger lines + update balance cache + write outbox row - all or nothing). DynamoDB transactions exist but are capped at 100 items and expensive; Cassandra can’t do this at all.💡 ACID is the database promise that a group of writes either all land or none do, and that other readers never see a half-finished group. An outbox row is a “publish this event later” row written inside that same group, so the event cannot go missing if the service dies a millisecond after committing.
  • SELECT FOR UPDATE on balance rows gives us row-level concurrency control for free.
  • Partitioning by month on ledger_lines keeps the hot set small as we grow; a single Postgres cluster comfortably handles tens of billions of rows with partitioning.
  • Auditors, finance tools, BI tools all speak SQL. A KV store makes daily reconciliation painful.
  • When we truly outgrow a single Postgres cluster (500M+ DAU, billions of transactions per day), we shard by user_id at the application layer and keep Postgres semantics. This is what Uber Gulfstream does.

Why Redis for balance cache (not just hitting Postgres):

  • Balance reads massively outnumber writes. Every app screen does a balance check.
  • Sub-ms reads matter for perceived app snappiness.
  • Postgres can handle it, but you’d burn half your cluster capacity on reads that have a 99.9% cache hit rate.

Why Cassandra / ClickHouse for history feed (not Postgres):

  • History is read-only after the write, and the access pattern is “latest N transactions for user X.”
  • Cassandra’s partition-per-user (user_id as partition key, created_at as clustering column) is tailor-made for this.
  • ClickHouse is better if we also want “top 1000 largest transactions today” - column-store aggregations.
  • Postgres works until ~100GB per table; past that, history queries start fighting OLTP writes.

Why Kafka as the event bus:

  • Ordering per user_id partition matters (notification for “you received money” must come after “send initiated”).
  • Replayability lets new consumers (fraud, analytics, new features) backfill from history.
  • Debezium plugs straight into Postgres WAL.

Data Modeling

Postgres (Ledger — source of truth, partitioned by month):

CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id UUID NOT NULL,
    account_type VARCHAR(20),  -- wallet_available, wallet_pending, platform_fee, tax
    balance DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00,
    currency VARCHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'INR',
    version BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0  -- optimistic lock for SELECT FOR UPDATE
);

CREATE TABLE journal_entries (
    entry_id BIGSERIAL,
    transaction_id UUID NOT NULL,
    account_id UUID NOT NULL,
    entry_type VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL,  -- DEBIT or CREDIT
    amount DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    -- Postgres requires every unique/primary key on a partitioned table to
    -- include the partition key, so created_at is part of the PK.
    PRIMARY KEY (entry_id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
-- Invariant: for every transaction_id, SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT)

CREATE TABLE transactions (
    transaction_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id UUID NOT NULL,
    type VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- CREDIT, DEBIT, P2P_SEND, P2P_RECEIVE, REFUND
    amount DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL,  -- PENDING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, REVERSED
    idempotency_key VARCHAR(128) UNIQUE,
    rail VARCHAR(20),  -- UPI, CARD, NEFT, WALLET
    counterparty_id UUID,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_txns_user ON transactions(user_id, created_at DESC);
SQL

Redis (Balance Cache — fast reads):

Key: "balance:{userId}" → Hash { available: "1500.00", pending: "200.00" }
Invalidated: on every ledger write (write-through or event-driven)
TTL: none (explicitly invalidated on mutation)

Redis (Idempotency Store):

Key: "idem:{userId}:{endpoint}:{idempotencyKey}" → JSON { transaction_id, status, response }
TTL: max_delay + 24 hours

Cassandra (Transaction History Feed — denormalized for fast reads):

Table: user_transactions
  PK: user_id
  SK: created_at (DESC)
  Columns: transaction_id, type, amount, status, counterparty_name, rail, description

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Check balance Redis HGETALL balance:{userId} — sub-ms
Credit wallet (add money) Postgres In txn: INSERT journal entries (DEBIT bank_inflow + CREDIT user_wallet) + UPDATE account balance + publish event
P2P transfer Postgres In txn: DEBIT sender + CREDIT receiver (2 journal entry pairs) — serializable isolation
Transaction history Cassandra Range scan user_transactions by user_id, paginate by created_at
Idempotency check Redis → Postgres Check Redis first (fast), fall back to transactions.idempotency_key unique index
scroll →

How a P2P Transfer Works at the Data Level (Double-Entry):

  1. Alice sends ₹500 to Bob → API checks idem:{alice}:transfer:{key} in Redis — not found, proceed
  2. BEGIN Postgres transaction:
  3. SELECT balance, version FROM accounts WHERE account_id = ? FOR UPDATE (Alice’s wallet) — locks the row
  4. Check: Alice.balance >= 500. If not: ROLLBACK, return insufficient funds
  5. INSERT INTO journal_entries — 4 rows: DEBIT Alice ₹500, CREDIT platform_transit ₹500, DEBIT platform_transit ₹500, CREDIT Bob ₹500
  6. UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE account_id = alice_wallet
  7. UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE account_id = bob_wallet
  8. INSERT INTO transactions (Alice’s record) + INSERT INTO transactions (Bob’s record)
  9. COMMIT — all 4 journal entries + 2 balance updates + 2 transaction records succeed atomically
  10. Async: invalidate Redis balance cache for both Alice and Bob, publish transaction.succeeded to Kafka, write to Cassandra history feed

Potential Deep Dives

1) How do we model money correctly so we don’t lose a rupee?

Problem. The defining question for a wallet. A naive “balance column” approach has been the cause of every “missing ₹1000 from my wallet” customer support ticket since the first digital wallets existed. Race conditions, unreconciled state, and one-sided updates all silently corrupt money.

Bad - what the high-level design built: a balance column that operations add to and subtract from. The arithmetic may well be right, and it is unfalsifiable, which where money is concerned is indistinguishable from being wrong. Asked why a user holds ₹4,320 the only available answer is “because the column says so”. Nothing records how it got there, so an off-by-one from a retried update is undetectable and permanent, and a customer disputing their balance cannot be answered either way. It also cannot answer the questions we are obliged to answer — what did this user hold at 3pm last Tuesday, how much of our float is money actually received versus still in flight, where did this particular ₹100 come from — because one mutable number keeps no history and separates no categories of money. The requirements name auditability as a target, and a mutable column is the one shape that cannot provide it.

The arithmetic may well be right, and it is unfalsifiable, which where money is concerned is indistinguishable from being wrong. Asked why a user holds ₹4,320 the only available answer is “because the column says so”. Nothing records how it got there, so an off-by-one from a retried update is undetectable and permanent, and a customer disputing their balance cannot be answered either way. It also cannot answer the questions we are obliged to answer — what did this user hold at 3pm last Tuesday, how much of our float is money actually received versus still in flight, where did this particular ₹100 come from — because one mutable number keeps no history and separates no categories of money. The requirements name auditability as a target, and a mutable column is the one shape that cannot provide it.

Append-only log of transfers: . Balance = . Much better. But it’s still only tracking ; it doesn’t model where money came from (which bank? which rail?) or where fees, promotions, and system money go.

Every money movement writes TWO balanced entries (debit one account, credit another). If debits don’t equal credits, the database rejects it — making it physically impossible to create or lose money. Balances are computed from these entries, never stored directly.

2) How do we handle concurrent transfers from the same user without corruption?


Problem. User A has ₹100. She taps “send ₹80 to B” and “send ₹50 to C” in rapid succession. Both land on different pods within milliseconds. Without concurrency control, both may pass a naive balance check (“₹100 > ₹80” and “₹100 > ₹50”) and proceed, leaving A with -₹30. Money has been created from nothing.


Bad - what FR2 built: read the balance, compare it, write the new one, with nothing holding the row in between.
A user with ₹100 taps “send ₹80 to B” and “send ₹50 to C” a moment apart. The requests land on
different pods, both read ₹100, both find it sufficient, and both commit. She has sent ₹130 she
never had and the system has created ₹30 from nothing, which is the exact failure the
non-functional requirements place above everything else. This is not an exotic interleaving:
double-tapping a send button is ordinary behaviour, and the gap between the read and the write is
wide enough that any concurrent request lands inside it. It is also silent. Both transfers succeed,
both recipients are paid, and the only evidence is a balance gone negative or a float that no
longer reconciles.

A user with ₹100 taps “send ₹80 to B” and “send ₹50 to C” a moment apart. The requests land on
different pods, both read ₹100, both find it sufficient, and both commit. She has sent ₹130 she
never had and the system has created ₹30 from nothing, which is the exact failure the
non-functional requirements place above everything else. This is not an exotic interleaving:
double-tapping a send button is ordinary behaviour, and the gap between the read and the write is
wide enough that any concurrent request lands inside it. It is also silent. Both transfers succeed,
both recipients are paid, and the only evidence is a balance gone negative or a float that no
longer reconciles.



The first transaction acquires a row lock; the second waits. By the time the second checks, it sees A’s balance reduced to ₹20 and fails correctly.


Implementation:




Works correctly. The table is a of the ledger; it’s the row we lock on for concurrency control. The truth is the ledger.


Problem: serializes concurrent transfers for that one user. Fine for retail users (one person can’t send 1000 transfers/sec). Not fine for a “platform account” that receives credits from millions of users.




 When user A sends money, we lock ONLY A’s row in the database. Other users’ transactions proceed in parallel unaffected. This prevents double-spending while keeping the system fast for everyone else.


For user accounts:


    
 
 



For (e.g., receiving credits from every transfer in the system):


    
 
 
 



For the ledger itself: journal_entries and ledger_lines are append-only with auto-increment IDs. No locks needed on writes; readers see a consistent snapshot.


 is correct but slow. Use (MySQL) or the default (Postgres) with explicit locks on the specific balance rows we care about. That’s the standard financial-system choice.




3) How do we serve balance reads at 100K+ QPS without hammering the ledger?


Problem. Every wallet screen on the app triggers a balance read. 100M active users checking their balance = catastrophic query load if we derive balance from scratch every time. But balance must be accurate, not stale, because it gates the next transfer.


Bad - the position Deep Dive 1 leaves us in: the mutable column is gone, so the balance is stored nowhere and must be summed on every read.
That is correct, auditable, and far too slow. A balance check now aggregates every ledger line the
user has ever accumulated, so the query cost grows with the length of the relationship and a
ten-year customer pays for a decade of their own history every time they open the app. This is the
most frequent read in the product — the requirements put it above 100K QPS against a 100ms target
— and FR2 also consults it before permitting any transfer, so it sits on the write path too. Deep
Dive 1 bought correctness by making the balance derived; leaving it there trades a correctness
problem for an availability one.

That is correct, auditable, and far too slow. A balance check now aggregates every ledger line the
user has ever accumulated, so the query cost grows with the length of the relationship and a
ten-year customer pays for a decade of their own history every time they open the app. This is the
most frequent read in the product — the requirements put it above 100K QPS against a 100ms target
— and FR2 also consults it before permitting any transfer, so it sits on the write path too. Deep
Dive 1 bought correctness by making the balance derived; leaving it there trades a correctness
problem for an availability one.



Single-row lookup per user. Correctness comes from the same DB transaction that writes the ledger lines - balance updates atomically with the underlying journal entry. Fast reads, guaranteed consistency.


This is already a huge win. Most real wallets stop here. But at PhonePe-scale (360M transactions/day, hundreds of thousands of balance reads/sec), even a single-row Postgres read is pressure on the primary.




 Instead of calculating balance from scratch every time (slow), we cache it in Redis. When a transaction happens, we update both the ledger (truth) and the cache (speed). If the cache fails, we fall back to computing from the ledger.


    
 
 
 



For platform accounts with skew (one account credited by millions of users), precompute running aggregates in a stream processor (Flink) subscribed to the ledger CDC stream; the query never touches the raw ledger.






    
 
 
 





4) How do we keep our wallet balances reconciled with the real money in our bank account?


Problem. Users trust our balance number. But that number is only valid if there’s real money in a partner bank account backing it. If our ledger says users collectively hold ₹100 crore in wallets, our bank partner must show ₹100 crore in our pooled account. Any drift is either a bug, a bank-side error, or fraud. Regulators require this reconciliation daily.💡 Reconciliation = comparing two independent records of the same money, ours and the bank’s, line by line and treating every unexplained difference as a defect to chase rather than noise. Nobody checking means the gap only surfaces when a regulator or a customer does the arithmetic for us. Learn more →


Bad - what FR1 built: credit the wallet on the strength of a callback and never check again.
Our records say what we believe happened; the partner bank’s records say what did. Those diverge
constantly, mostly for dull reasons — a charge reversed after we were told it succeeded, a
settlement landing a day later than modelled, a fee deducted we never accounted for, a webhook that
never arrived and left a transaction PENDING forever. None of it is fraud and all of it is
invisible here, because nothing in the design ever compares the two sides. The gap compounds
quietly, and because users spend against the figure we hold, it is not a reporting discrepancy but
real money we have promised and may not have. It surfaces when somebody else does the arithmetic
for us: a regulator, or a customer whose bank statement disagrees with our app.

Our records say what we believe happened; the partner bank’s records say what did. Those diverge
constantly, mostly for dull reasons — a charge reversed after we were told it succeeded, a
settlement landing a day later than modelled, a fee deducted we never accounted for, a webhook that
never arrived and left a transaction forever. None of it is fraud and all of it is
invisible here, because nothing in the design ever compares the two sides. The gap compounds
quietly, and because users spend against the figure we hold, it is not a reporting discrepancy but
real money we have promised and may not have. It surfaces when somebody else does the arithmetic
for us: a regulator, or a customer whose bank statement disagrees with our app.



Every night, pull the bank’s statement for our pooled account, compute our expected balance from the ledger (), compare. Alert on mismatch.


Works and is legally required. But “we find the break 24 hours later” is too slow - you may have millions more transactions stacked on top of a broken state.




Three layers of defense:


    
 
 
 



Real-world example patterns:


    
 
 
 





5) How do we prevent double-debiting on retries and across services?


Problem. Network failures are guaranteed. A user taps “send ₹500” - their phone’s radio drops mid-request. Their app retries. Without idempotency, we debit them twice. If our own internal services retry (e.g., Payment Gateway adapter timing out), we may charge the bank twice.


Bad - what FR1 and FR2 built: no request carries any identifier for the intent behind it.
A user taps send, the phone loses signal before the response lands, and the app retries — which is
what a well-written client should do. We see a second, entirely valid-looking transfer and execute
it. She sent ₹500 twice and meant it once. The same hole exists on the way in: a rail that delivers
its webhook twice, or delivers it just as our own status check asks the same question, credits the
load twice. Because each request is individually correct, nothing warns and nothing fails, so we
learn about it when the customer does. Retries are not an exceptional path here either — every
timeout in a network that includes banks produces one, so at any real volume duplicate processing
is scheduled rather than merely possible.💡 This is what “at-least-once delivery” means: a sender that cannot tell whether its message arrived will send it again, so duplicates are the normal case, not the exception. The only way to get an exactly-once effect is for the receiver to recognise and drop repeats. Learn more →

A user taps send, the phone loses signal before the response lands, and the app retries — which is
what a well-written client should do. We see a second, entirely valid-looking transfer and execute
it. She sent ₹500 twice and meant it once. The same hole exists on the way in: a rail that delivers
its webhook twice, or delivers it just as our own status check asks the same question, credits the
load twice. Because each request is individually correct, nothing warns and nothing fails, so we
learn about it when the customer does. Retries are not an exceptional path here either — every
timeout in a network that includes banks produces one, so at any real volume duplicate processing
is scheduled rather than merely possible.



Client sends a UUID; server checks . Duplicates return the original response.




 Every request gets a unique key. If the same request arrives twice (network retry), we recognize the key and return the same result without processing again. No double-charges, ever.


Lifted directly from Airbnb’s production design:


    
 
 
 



Rules:


    
 
 



Plus two critical pieces Airbnb calls out:


 Every failed operation is stamped with its retryability:


    
 
 



Misclassification is how you get stuck transactions or double-debits. Every new exception type gets reviewed for retry semantics.


 Never check the idempotency table on a read replica. Replica lag between a write and a retry is exactly the window where you accidentally process twice. This is a subtle bug with huge blast radius.


 Loads and withdrawals span multiple seconds. If the Transaction row is picked up for reconciliation while another process is mid-flight, you need optimistic locking - . Zero rows updated = someone else beat you, retry.


Downstream processors (card rails, UPI, bank APIs) should also receive a deterministic idempotency key derived from our transaction ID - - so even if we retry, the external system dedupes.




6) Balance > 0 but can’t spend it: how do we model holds, pending, and available balance?


Problem. A user loads ₹500. The bank says “pending” for up to 2 business days. Should the user see ₹500 in their available balance? No - we haven’t actually received the money yet. Similarly, if a user sends ₹100 that hasn’t cleared the recipient’s bank-linked rail yet, that’s in flight. We need to distinguish provisional balance from available balance.


Bad - what FR1 and FR3 built: a single balance figure with no notion of whether the money has actually arrived.
FR1 step 7 adds a load to balance as soon as the rail reports success, but for a direct bank debit
“success” can mean the transfer has been accepted and will settle in up to two business days. The
user sees ₹500 and can spend it at once, against money we do not hold — and if that debit later
fails we have already let it out of the door. The mirror case is no better: withholding everything
unsettled means a user watching money sit in the app that is genuinely theirs and untouchable. One
number cannot express both “this is yours” and “this is not spendable yet”, and no amount of care in
the services above it recovers a distinction the data model does not make.

FR1 step 7 adds a load to as soon as the rail reports success, but for a direct bank debit
“success” can mean the transfer has been and will settle in up to two business days. The
user sees ₹500 and can spend it at once, against money we do not hold — and if that debit later
fails we have already let it out of the door. The mirror case is no better: withholding everything
unsettled means a user watching money sit in the app that is genuinely theirs and untouchable. One
number cannot express both “this is yours” and “this is not spendable yet”, and no amount of care in
the services above it recovers a distinction the data model does not make.



Store both on the cached row. is what they can spend; is inflow that hasn’t cleared.


Works for simple cases. Falls apart with refunds, disputes, stuck transactions, and long-tail edge cases. Ends up needing more fields.




Every user has multiple sub-accounts:


    
 
 
 
 



Transfers between these are ledger entries. “Clearing” a pending load is a ledger entry: debit , credit . Nothing special. Holds, releases, and clears are all expressible as balanced journal entries.




    
 
 
 
 



This is how Venmo, Cash App, and Stripe all model it internally.




Core Flows


Flow 1 - Peer-to-peer transfer




    
 
  1. Sender app generates a UUIDv4 idempotency key tied to the tap action and retries with the same key.
    2. 
 
  2. Transfer Service checks Redis for the idempotency key. Duplicate retries replay the cached response - no double-debit.
    3. 
 
  3. Pre-RPC phase begins: lock sender’s balance row with SELECT FOR UPDATE.
    4. 
 
  4. Validate sufficient funds, daily limit, KYC tier, recipient is valid.
    5. 
 
  5. Insert the journal entry and two ledger lines (debit sender, credit recipient) PLUS an outbox row in one atomic tx. This is the core correctness guarantee: both halves of the money move atomically.
    6. 
 
  6. Update the cached balance rows in the same tx.
    7. 
 
  7. Commit. Response returns to sender. Debezium drains outbox to Kafka, fanning out to notifications, history store, analytics.
    8. 



Failure: if FOR UPDATE times out waiting on another transaction (user in rapid succession), we return 429 Retry and the client retries with the same key - idempotency guarantees no duplicate on retry.


Flow 2 - Load money from bank




    
 
  1. App sends load with an idempotency key and payment instrument ID.
    2. 
 
  2. Wallet Service inserts Transaction row in PENDING before any network call.
    3. 
 
  3. Calls the payment gateway. On success, journal entry is posted: DEBIT rail_receivable, CREDIT user_wallet. User sees balance increase.
    4. 
 
  4. On timeout, Transaction stays PENDING. Crucially, no ledger entry exists yet - money has not been declared to exist. User sees “pending” in app.
    5. 
 
  5. Reconciler polls the bank every 30s for any PENDING transaction older than 2 min and makes a definitive call.
    6. 



Later, when the bank actually settles (1-2 business days), a separate ledger entry reconciles rail_receivable to cash_in_bank. This is the audit-critical piece.


Flow 3 - Withdraw to bank


Structurally symmetric to Load. Debit user_wallet, credit rail_payable immediately (freezing the user’s balance). The physical money movement to their bank is async via the rail; on confirmation, we debit rail_payable and credit cash_in_bank (reducing our bank holdings). On bank failure, we reverse: debit rail_payable, credit user_wallet, restoring the user’s balance. Every step is a balanced journal entry, so the audit trail is bulletproof.


Transaction state machine




Every transition is a compare-and-set in the DB and emits an event. Illegal transitions no-op silently (update 0 rows).




Final Architecture




How it works end-to-end:


    
 
  1. User initiates transaction — Wallet App sends request through API Gateway to Wallet Service or Transfer Service
    2. 
 
  2. Idempotency validated — Redis idem cache rejects duplicate requests before any state change
    3. 
 
  3. Ledger writes double-entry — Ledger Service persists balanced debit + credit entries to Postgres primary with row-level locking
    4. 
 
  4. External rail called if needed — Payment Gateway Adapters charge or credit the bank/UPI
    5. 
 
  5. CDC streams changes — Debezium captures write-ahead log (WAL) changes and publishes to Kafka💡 The write-ahead log is the ordered record a database appends to before applying any change, so reading it gives you every committed write in commit order. Debezium is one tool that tails Postgres’s log and republishes it as events. Learn more →
    6. 
 
  6. Downstream consumers update — Kafka feeds balance cache (Redis), hot balance reads (Aerospike), transaction history (Cassandra), and triggers notifications
    7. 
 
  7. Read path serves fast — Read Service checks Redis balance cache first, falls back to Postgres read replica and Cassandra for history
    8. 
 
  8. Reconciler ensures integrity — polls bank rails daily, compares with internal ledger, fixes discrepancies
    9. 



That’s the design. Six deep dives each picking the right primitive: double-entry ledger with chart-of-accounts for correctness, row-locking with FOR UPDATE plus partitioned platform accounts for concurrency, tiered balance caches for read scale, continuous-plus-daily reconciliation for integrity with real banks, Orpheus-style three-phase idempotency to kill double-debits, and modeling holds as first-class accounts instead of flags. Correctness first, everything else second - a wallet that occasionally loses money is not a wallet.




Key Technologies Mentioned



 
 

 Term
 What it is
 

 
 
 

 Double-entry Ledger
 Accounting model where every money movement creates balanced debit + credit entries that sum to zero - money can never be created or destroyed.
 

 

 Idempotency Key
 Client-generated UUID attached to every payment request ensuring retries produce the same result without double-charging.
 

 

 Saga Pattern
 Sequence of local transactions with compensating actions (e.g., refund) used when operations span multiple services that can’t share a DB transaction.
 

 

 Optimistic Locking (CAS)
 Compare-and-swap via a version column - UPDATE succeeds only if the version matches, detecting concurrent modifications without holding locks.
 

 

 Materialized Balance
 A cached running total derived from the ledger; updated atomically with ledger writes and used for fast balance checks.
 

 

 Reconciliation
 Periodic comparison of internal ledger state against external bank statements to detect and resolve discrepancies.
 

 

 Kafka
 Distributed event bus carrying transaction events (via CDC/outbox) to notifications, analytics, and the history feed.
 

 

 Postgres
 ACID relational database serving as the ledger source of truth with row-level locking for concurrency control on balances.

What’s Expected at Each Level



 
This section helps you calibrate your depth. You don’t need to cover everything - just know what’s expected for your level.




Mid-level


Design a basic wallet with balance storage and transfer capability. Understand why double-spend is the core problem - two concurrent requests draining the same balance must not both succeed. Propose database transactions for atomic balance updates and explain why check-then-deduct is a race condition.


Senior


Propose double-entry ledger (every transaction creates two entries: debit + credit). Explain idempotency keys for safe retries without double-charging. Discuss saga pattern for multi-party transfers involving external banks and reconciliation with external payment gateways. Articulate why eventual consistency is unacceptable for balance operations.


Staff+


Address distributed ledger consistency across shards (partitioned platform accounts to avoid hot-key contention). Discuss settlement and clearing processes with partner banks, regulatory compliance (PCI-DSS, RBI guidelines for prepaid instruments), and fraud detection patterns (velocity checks, device fingerprinting). Cover how to handle partial failures in multi-step payment flows using three-phase idempotency and the cost of strong consistency at scale.




🎯 Key Takeaways


    
 
  • Double-entry ledger - every transaction has debit + credit; sum must be zero
    • 
 
  • Persist before calling external - write intent to DB, then call bank; never the reverse
    • 
 
  • Idempotency key on every payment - retries are safe
    • 
 
  • Reconciler compares our ledger with bank statements daily
    •
